newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Transport Council to focus on EU applicants.
newsitem.headline: Transport Council to focus on EU applicants.

text.p: Thursday's Transport Council in Luxembourg will be marked by the likely adoption of a European Commission mandate to negotiate aviation relations with the central and east European countries.

Aside from this matter (see BC-AVIATION-EAST, MOVED OCT 1), ministers are not due to take any final decisions as such, with much of the work destined to be preparatory given the earliness of the meeting in Ireland's Council presidency.

One file which has been around for a while, namely negotiations between the EU and Switzerland on land transport, will be the subject of discussion in a progress report from the Commission. This is likely to prompt debate on the wider implications for internal EU policy (see BC-TRANSPORT-SWITZERLAND, MOVED OCT 1).
Ministers will also have their second meeting with their counterparts from the central and east European countries as part of the structured dialogue.
This meeting, which follows the first such get-together in September last year, will include a Commission report on transport infrastructure needs in the applicant countries.
Ministers will then discuss possibilities for common policies on rail and bimodal transport for the countries involved. A second item will be policy on transport tariffs.

Council thoughts will then return closer to the present with talks on Transport Commissioner Kinnock's July 1996 proposals to revise Directive 93/89/EEC. This comes in the light of European Court of Justice rulings on the original directive and the Commission's latest thinking on pricing road hauliers according to an assessment of the damage they cause to infrastructure.
"This is quite a new proposal and quite a major rethink of taxation policy," a spokesman for the Council of Ministers President told reporters earlier this week.
Among the main points is a suggestion for differentiated taxation according to lorry type along the lines suggested in Kinnock's green paper on transport pricing.
For this file, as for many others on the agenda, talks will be very much a sighting shot for ministers' future debates.
Another orientation debate will take place on a draft regulation on the access conditions to EU road passenger markets for non-national transport companies.
Negotiations will take place to the backdrop of the Court's annulment of Regulation 2454/92, a legal instrument which remains in place while the replacement is prepared.
The part of the Commission's proposal which is going nowhere relates to cabotage for scheduled services.
"Given the position of a majority of member states against the liberalisation of purely internal cabotage, this part of the file will not be dealt with," one EU diplomat said.
Positions on the question of cabotage for international scheduled services are "more nuanced", the diplomat added.
Ministers will also have an orientation debate on a proposal COM(96)190 to simplify procedures for international carriage of passengers by bus and coach, as currently defined by Regulation 684/92.

The Council will also hear a Kinnock presentation on the Commission's recent white paper on the future of the railways system, COM(96)421, which sets out proposals to revitalise the sector, particularly as it concerns freight carriage.
Ministers will also tackle Commission proposal COM(95)724 for a regulation on air carriers' accident liability, for which the European Parliament completed its first reading in September.

One of the parliament's amendments, if retained by the European Commission and the Council of Ministers, would raise the limit for carriers' objective liability compensation by 20,000 Ecus to 120,000 Ecus per passenger.

The Commission proposal sets out to abolish existing Warsaw Convention limits on air carrier liability; to lay down the principle of objective liability up to the sum of 100,000 Ecus; to set up a system of emergency payments for relatives of killed or injured passengers and; to allow victims or their relatives to bring liability court actions in their own countries.

Finally, on Friday's maritime transport agenda, ministers will discuss the proposal COM(96)255) for a Council directive setting up a harmonised safety regime for fishing vessels of 24 metres or more in length.
